claim: The Great Sphinx is described by the Egyptian Ministry as carved directly from the bedrock during Dynasty 4.

Perring described the burial chamber as excavated in rock with an angular roof of compact stone blocks extending into the rock beyond the chamber sides.
Perring recorded the sarcophagus sunk into the western floor zone, surrounded by large granite blocks and bedded on a granite slab in cement.
Perring recorded rectangular holes in the north and south sides of the burial chamber and red traced outlines beneath them; their purpose was uncertain.

Perring reported a wall stain interpreted as evidence that water had once stood about 12 inches deep in the lower chamber. This is a nineteenth-century condition observation, not a modern groundwater measurement.
The British Museum records that Belzoni discovered the entrance and passages leading to Khafre’s burial chamber on 2 March 1818.
The Met identifies the original red-granite architrave as made for Khafre and probably from the court of his pyramid temple at Giza.
The Met records later reuse of the original Khafre architrave in the entrance corridor of Amenemhat I’s pyramid at Lisht, more than five centuries later.
The Met attributes the fragmentary royal face to Khafre based on find context, royal-beard traces and similarity to temple statues.
Memphis and its Necropolis, including the Giza pyramid fields, was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979.

AERA interprets the south side of the Sphinx quarry as respecting an already-existing Khafre causeway foundation, placing the causeway before the Sphinx quarry in relative sequence.
AERA sequences the Khafre Valley Temple before the Sphinx Temple because a Valley Temple enclosure wall was later incorporated into the Sphinx Temple.
AERA’s re-excavation found Area C mostly empty with activity near gallery entrances and proposed storage/craft use rather than worker barracks, probably during Khafre construction.
